Beyond the results above, we provide fine-grained characterizations of dense generation under o(1)-noise and c-noise regimes. These results, summarized in Table 1, characterize which countable collections admit dense generation under various contamination models. Notably, two characterizations remain open: while we establish impossibility for arbitrary countable collections (Theorem 32), complete characterizations for these cases are interesting directions. We also observe several qualitative phenomena. First, while set-based lower and upper densities have distinct characterizations without contamination (Kleinberg and Wei, 2025a), they collapse to a single characterization under contamination. Second, as noted before, elementbased density is notably more contamination-tolerant than set-based density (Informal Theorem 8).

Note (⋆) This result is stronger: it tolerates finite noise with infinite omissions, provided omissions are not too dense (c-omissions; Appendix F). See Theorems 17 and 18. A general takeaway is that dense generation is much less contamination-tolerant than non-dense generation, contrasting (Kleinberg and Wei, 2025a)’s positive results, which suggested density was achievable whenever generation was. Beyond Worst-Case Adversaries (Appendix D). We also study a restricted adversarial model inspired by curriculum learning (Bengio et al., 2009): An adversary is M -bounded if, for sufficiently large n, any xn ∈ K it enumerates satisfies xn = κi for some i ≤ M n, where κ1 , κ2 , . . . is the canonical enumeration of K. Intuitively, if we order the elements of the language starting from easier ones to harder ones, then such adversaries cannot present “hard” elements far before “easier” ones. Under this model, dense generation becomes significantly more tractable: all countable collections admit set-based and element-based lower density Ω(1/M ) under o(1)-noise and arbitrary omissions, and these bounds are tight up to a factor of 2 (Theorems 39 and 40). This contrasts sharply with arbitrary adversaries, where no density notion is universally achievable even under arbitrarily sparse infinite contamination.

Our first algorithmic template is quite simple and enables us to achieve dense and non-dense generation with finite contamination. The algorithm relies on the following elementary observation: If the enumeration E generated by the adversary has finite contamination, then it must be a 0-contamination enumeration of a language K ′ satisfying with |K ′ △K| < ∞. Now, of course, K ′ might not be a language in our collection L , but the natural thing to do is to add K ′ to L . We will need to add all possible choices since we do not know K ′ in advance. Then, we end up with the following collection f:= {LA,B := L ∪ A \ B : L ∈ L , A ⊆ Σ∗ \ L, B ⊆ L, |A| < ∞, |B| < ∞} , L where Σ∗ is the universe of strings. Since the number of finite subsets of a countable collection are countable, Lfis a countable collection. This immediately gives us an algorithm for generation with finite amounts of contamination since we can use (Kleinberg and Mullainathan, 2024)’s algorithm that works for all countable collections with L finstead of L . This simple idea yields clean analyses while offering many useful properties that make it widely applicable; including but not limited to: ▷ As we have seen, it preserves countability (if L is countable, so is L f). ▷ Further, membership access to L is sufficient to get membership6 access to L f. ▷ In several contamination regimes and density measures, if G achieves density with respect to L it also achieves density with respect to L ′ . This transformation also preserves generation with approximate breadth, which is a stronger notion than density introduced in Kalavasis et al. (2025). We leverage such properties in our results, and we believe there may be additional benefits. For instance, points 1 and 2 above together allow us to get a membership oracle-based algorithm for generation with finite contamination (Corollary 9) that resolves an open question from Raman and Raman (2025); it is unclear how to resolve it using using prior techniques. Priority-Based Intersection Algorithm (Appendix A.1). Next, we discuss our algorithms for the much more involved case where the amount of contamination is infinite. We begin by explaining why earlier approaches fail: ▷ The previous simple approach that constructs the “expanded” collection L f fails because the collection L becomes uncountable (if the amount of noise is not finite) and not all uncountable f collections are generable in the limit, even without the requirement of density. The situation with density is even more complicated as the transformation is no longer density preserving. ▷ Another idea is to use approaches from Raman and Raman (2025); Bai et al. (2026). Raman and Raman (2025) use a nice observation for generating in the limit: if the amount of noise is finite then, for sufficiently large n, the second half of the training examples (namely, {xn/2 , xn/2+1 , . . . , xn }) eventually contains no noisy examples. Hence, roughly speaking, feeding the second half of the examples to an appropriate generation algorithm suffices. This, of course, fails when there is an infinite amount of noisy examples in the stream. Bai et al. (2026) make another nice observation: if G has the property that it generates from L after n⋆ = n⋆ (K) iterations, where n⋆ depends on the target K, but not on its enumeration, then G generates from L in the limit under arbitrary omissions (provided there is no noise). statement: There are several interesting future directions related to noisy generation, and more broadly, the line of work on generation in the limit. An interesting direction is to fully characterize elementbased generation for all types of contamination model we study. Further, our finite-contamination algorithm uses only membership oracle access to L , but several of our other algorithms require more powerful oracles; understanding what can be achieved with simpler oracles remains open. Finally, beyond restricting the adversary, another way to circumvent our lower bounds may be to relax the learner’s requirements: how does the landscape of (noisy) generation change if the generator may output a vanishing fraction of hallucinations? We note that a similar question was posed by Kleinberg and Wei (2025a) in the context of improving density guarantees.
context: 6. Discussion and Open Problems In this work, we characterized the contamination tolerance of language generation in the limit (Theorems 5 and 7 and Informal Theorem 8). We showed that standard generation can tolerate contamination in infinite quantity, only requiring that the fraction of contaminated examples converges to zero. Dense generation, in contrast, can only tolerate finite amounts of contamination. Thus, the additional coverage guarantees of dense generation come at a cost in robustness. There are several interesting future directions related to noisy generation, and more broadly, the line of work on generation in the limit. An interesting direction is to fully characterize elementbased generation for all types of contamination model we study. Further, our finite-contamination algorithm uses only membership oracle access to L , but several of our other algorithms require more powerful oracles; understanding what can be achieved with simpler oracles remains open. Finally, beyond restricting the adversary, another way to circumvent our lower bounds may be to relax the learner’s requirements: how does the landscape of (noisy) generation change if the generator may output a vanishing fraction of hallucinations? We note that a similar question was posed by Kleinberg and Wei (2025a) in the context of improving density guarantees.
